questions.stem: An in-house LP code accepts only max c·x subject to Ax ≤ b with x ≥ 0. Your model minimizes x + 3y subject to 2x − y ≥ 6, with x, y ≥ 0. What do you hand the code?

options.text: The row −2x + y ≤ −6 and the objective max −x − 3y
options.says: Right: the >= row is multiplied by −1 on both sides, and min f is max −f.

options.text: The row −2x + y ≤ 6 and the objective max −x − 3y
options.says: Multiplying by −1 flips the right-hand side too: it is −6.

options.text: The row 2x − y ≤ 6 and the objective max x + 3y
options.says: Turning >= into <= without negating changes which points are allowed, and max x + 3y is a different goal.

options.text: The row −2x + y ≤ −6 and the objective max x + 3y
options.says: The row is right, but a minimization becomes a maximization of the negated objective.

origin.section: Every LP Can Be Rewritten Into One Standard Form

questions.stem: At an LP's optimum, a crew row 0.004·s ≤ 12 has activity 9, and a floor row v ≥ 250 has v = 250. How do you describe the two rows?

options.text: The crew row is binding with slack 3; the floor row has surplus 250
options.says: A row with room 3 is not binding, and the floor's surplus is v − 250 = 0.

options.text: The crew row has surplus 3; the floor row is binding with slack 0
options.says: Room on a <= row is called slack, and on a >= row surplus, not the other way round.

options.text: The crew row has slack 3; the floor row is binding with surplus 0
options.says: Right: slack is 12 − 9 on the <= row; surplus is 250 − 250 on the >= row.

options.text: The crew row has slack −3; the floor row has surplus 250
options.says: Slack is bound minus activity, 12 − 9 = 3, never negative for an allowed solution.

origin.section: Slack Is the Room Left in a ≤ Row, and Surplus Is the Excess Over a ≥ Row

questions.stem: At the optimum of a program-split LP, a regulator's floor row has surplus 40, while the budget row has slack 0. The regulator drops the floor entirely. What happens to the optimal value?

options.text: It rises, because removing any rule lets the split earn more
options.says: Removing a rule can only help, but here the floor had room, so the old optimum stays best.

options.text: It falls, because the split loses a row it was resting on
options.says: Removing a row never removes allowed splits, so the value cannot fall.

options.text: It cannot be told without solving again from scratch
options.says: A row with room is not holding the answer, so the outcome is known without a re-solve.

options.text: It stays the same, because the floor was not holding the answer
options.says: Right: a row with room does not shape the answer; loosening or deleting it changes nothing.

origin.section: A Row With Room Does Not Shape the Answer; Loosening It Changes Nothing
